quotes.text: Transformation is not the installation of a new capability. It is the redistribution of who gets to act, who gets to decide, and who gets to access the information they need.
quotes.speaker: Mirko Peters
quotes.why: Concise redefinition of transformation as a shift of authority rather than a tool rollout.

quotes.text: Policy without adherence is not control, it is just documentation, and documentation can create a false sense of safety.
quotes.speaker: Mirko Peters
quotes.why: Sharp warning against mistaking governance documents for real control.

quotes.text: If those roles are still unclear, then all AI has done is increase the speed of ambiguity and speed without clarity is not transformation, it's amplification.
quotes.speaker: Mirko Peters
quotes.why: Explains why AI amplifies unclear accountability instead of fixing it.

quotes.text: Permissions should match accountability. It doesn't have to be perfect in every single edge case, but it must be true structurally.
quotes.speaker: Mirko Peters
quotes.why: Clear design principle for aligning access with responsibility.

quotes.text: If your permissions are messy, co-pilot turns that into a trust issue. If your content is stale, duplicated or context poor, co-pilot turns that into weak output.
quotes.speaker: Mirko Peters
quotes.why: Shows concretely how Copilot mirrors weaknesses in permissions and content.

takeaways: Transformations stall when tools change but decision rights, ownership and access paths stay the same.
Copilot, Teams, SharePoint and Power Platform act as structural tests that expose weak ownership, misaligned permissions and hidden bottlenecks.
Start with one value stream, map decisions, dependencies, ownership and access, redesign approvals and escalation, and measure decision latency and cycle time before scaling.
hook: Many Microsoft 365 and Copilot programs show high adoption while the business still feels slow and political. This episode is for leaders and architects who want to understand why, and introduces the power architect as the missing responsibility for redesigning how authority, access and decisions flow.
